props.title: Prick Up Your Ears
props.initialSlug: Gay playwright's rise ends in deadly obsession

sections.content: Prick Up Your Ears delivers a searing portrait of playwright Joe Orton and his turbulent relationship with Kenneth Halliwell, anchored by Gary Oldman's electric performance. Director Stephen Frears crafts a brutally honest look at 1960s London's literary scene and gay subculture, following similar territory to his earlier My Beautiful Laundrette (1985). The film's unflinching approach to sexuality and creative ambition set a template for later LGBTQ+ biopics like Gods and Monsters (1998) and Love Is the Devil (1998).

sections.content: The film masterfully captures the charged creative partnership between Orton and Halliwell, reminiscent of other toxic artistic relationships depicted in Amadeus (1984) and Total Eclipse (1995). Alfred Molina's portrayal of Halliwell's descent into jealousy and madness provides a devastating counterpoint to Oldman's ascending star, creating tension that rivals Sid and Nancy (1986), another Oldman tour de force from the same era.

Director Stephen Frears employs a sophisticated narrative structure, using Vanessa Redgrave's literary agent as both participant and observer, similar to the technique used in The Usual Suspects (1995). The film's exploration of class mobility through art connects to other British works like An Education (2009) and The History Boys (2006). SUBHEAD: British New Wave Connections

sections.content: Prick Up Your Ears belongs to a vital tradition of British films examining class, sexuality, and artistic ambition, alongside works like Sunday Bloody Sunday (1971) and Maurice (1987). The film's portrayal of working-class intellectuals and sexual outsiders connects directly to the British New Wave's kitchen sink dramas, while its dark humor and theatrical elements presage later works like The Crying Game (1992) and Velvet Goldmine (1998).
